01Rationale

Why this level matters

An agent is a system component that makes decisions at run time, which changes how you design, test and secure everything around it. This level treats agents as architecture, not as a feature: what they may do, what they must never do, how you know they work, and how you stop them. Its scope is informed by current research and the iSAQB CPSA-A AGENTA module, Architecture for Agentic Software Engineering Contexts; Intellica’s curriculum and credential remain independent.

External reference: iSAQB CPSA-A AGENTA — Architecture for Agentic Software Engineering Contexts. The published module awards 10 technological and 20 methodical credit points within the CPSA-A scheme. Intellica's level is independently designed and does not confer iSAQB credit or accreditation.

02Target competencies

Intended learning outcomes

Choose the right shape

Decide when a fixed workflow is better than an agent, and how much autonomy to grant.

Design the boundaries

Define tools, permissions, memory and budgets for an agent system.

Prove it works

Plan evaluations and tracing so you can measure an agent, not just watch it.

Document for agents

Write architecture notes that people and coding agents can both read.

03Planned scope

Proposed scope: 12 lessons in 3 modules

This outline describes the intended curriculum. Lesson materials and assessments are not yet available.

Module 1Agents as components

What an agent is, architecturally.

  1. Workflows and agents: choosing between them
  2. Tools as contracts
  3. Levels of autonomy
  4. Context and memory

Module 2Designing agent systems

Patterns, limits and failure.

  1. Orchestration patterns
  2. Human approval and handover
  3. Failure modes, retries and cost budgets
  4. Multi-agent systems: when they help and when they do not

Module 3Making them trustworthy

Evidence, visibility and safety.

  1. Evaluation plans
  2. Observability and tracing
  3. Security boundaries and prompt injection
  4. Documenting an agent architecture

04Planned practical work

Your agent system design

Proposed project: Design and document an agent system for a real task in your own field, with limits you can defend. This practical component will be developed and validated before the level opens.

The steps

  1. Describe the task and decide workflow or agent
  2. Define the tools and their contracts
  3. Set permissions, budgets and approval points
  4. Design the memory and context
  5. Write the evaluation plan
  6. Write the architecture note an agent could read

Intended validation criteria

  • Every tool has a contract and a permission
  • There is a stated limit on cost and on actions
  • The evaluation plan names a measurable pass mark

05How you learn

Proposed learning design

Worked examples

The professional academies begin with complete examples and make the reasoning behind good decisions visible.

Guided practice

Scaffolds fade as learners progress—from annotated examples to structured tasks and independent work.

Retrieval and review

Low-stakes questions prompt recall; review revisits important concepts. Model answers and rubrics make improvement specific.

Research-informed updates

The academies cite primary research and standards, record review dates and receive versioned updates as evidence changes.

The proposed learning design draws on retrieval practice, worked examples and spaced review; detailed learner materials will be published before release. Read the evidence and sources.

06Intended audience

What it builds on

Level 3, Quality, Decisions and Evaluation, or equivalent experience designing systems against quality goals.
